source.title: Scaling Vision Transformers
source.authors: Xiao-Hua Zhai; Alexander Kolesnikov; N. Houlsby; Lucas Beyer

page_placements.theme: Model scale and pretraining can improve sample efficiency

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in image models, a new modality relative to the language-model scaling claims. The measured outcomes are image-transfer error rates, not held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper measures transfer error across model, data, and compute scales. It reports scaling-law fits and results on several image datasets. It does not measure language-model loss or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Detailed checkpoint results in Appendix Tables 4–22 are not reproduced as individual rows here; the rows focus on the reported scaling frontiers and explicit shape qualifications.
record.test_reason: The study fits saturating power laws to ViT image-classification transfer error against training compute, across model, data and training-duration scales. This bears on V5 (power-law form in another modality). It does not measure language-model loss, so V1–V4, V6 and V7, which concern language-model systems, are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the ViT performance-compute frontier, given enough data, roughly follows a saturating power law. Staying on the frontier requires scaling model size with compute. Larger models are more sample efficient and strong few-shot learners. Conclusions may not generalise beyond the studied scale or the ViT family.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales vision transformers and measures image-transfer error rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy. Its frontier is a saturating power law over model, data, and compute choices; it does not test language-model parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on model capacity, dataset size, training duration, and transfer evaluation setting; the paper reports differing behavior for few-shot and fine-tuning evaluations and imperfect fits on Pets.

fits_no_version.finding: Bigger ViTs are more sample efficient: Ti/16 needs about 100x more images than L/16 for 10-shot, and about 20x when fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision transformers, larger models reach a given transfer error with fewer training images.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling patch size and resolution together at fixed token count barely changes ImageNet 10-shot accuracy (e.g. B/32 64.43, B/48 64.65, B/64 64.67; Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ViT transfer quality depends mainly on token count, not on the patch/resolution split.

record.problems: The scaling-law study uses proprietary JFT-3B data, with ImageNet-21k as a public-data check. The paper itself cautions against generalizing beyond its tested scale and ViT family. Some fits are imperfect, and uncertainty estimates are not reported for the plotted scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Tables 4–22 contain many checkpoint-level few-shot and fine-tuning results by dataset size, training steps, cooldown, and learning rate; these detailed values were not separately extracted. The rows retain the reported aggregate scaling relationships, the explicitly identified imperfect fits, and the sample-efficiency comparison.

untested.parts: Upstream (pretraining) loss of the image models is not reported; only transfer error is. Video, repeated-data and language fine-tuning regimes are not tested.
No test of predicting much larger runs from fits on small runs.
No language-model shape study. The ViT patch/resolution comparison is recorded under fits_no_version.
No language-model downstream tasks, and no downstream-versus-pretraining-loss relation.
No comparison of fitting choices or of published language-model laws.

missing.what: Error versus model size (data and compute unconstrained) and error versus dataset size: small models saturate regardless of data; the largest models still improve from 1B to 3B images; L/16 stalls near 27% on 30M versus 19% on larger data.
Fitted equation coefficients for each Figure 9 panel, e.g. Pets exponents near 0.72–0.77 against about 0.2–0.4 elsewhere (panel mapping garbled in the text).

record.verdict_notes: The measure is downstream transfer error of discriminative image models, not pretraining loss. V6 and V7 links were removed because those versions concern language-model systems; the saturation finding is recorded as a V5 scope limit. The scaling data are proprietary (JFT-3B), with ImageNet-21k as a public check. No uncertainty is reported on the fits.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns vision models and transfer error, not held-out language-model pretraining loss.
It does not test whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
It does not fit a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation trend.
The study does not measure loss at fixed parameter count while systematically varying depth and width. Its resolution/patch-size comparison concerns transfer accuracy.
Tests image-model scaling using transfer error rates; does not test video, repeated-data language training, fine-tuning or transfer as training regimes for language-model pretraining loss.
Tests image downstream transfer performance against compute and training scale; does not test language-model downstream tasks or downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
The study reports saturation and imperfect fits, but does not test whether language-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on parameter counting, schedules, data, or fitting method.

rows.subject: ViT models (Pareto frontier)
rows.size_stated: Models range from five million to two billion parameters
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on image classification data; evaluated by linear 10-shot transfer
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size, dataset size, and training duration; plotted transfer error against total training compute.
rows.value: The Pareto frontier follows a power-law relationship with compute for over two orders of magnitude; a saturating power law is described as an accurate approximation.
rows.note: This is representation-transfer error, not pretraining cross-entropy. The frontier uses the best allocation of compute to model shape and training duration.
rows.check: Drop V6: V6 concerns downstream performance of language models, and this is a vision system. The value omits the fitted law E = 0.12 + 0.63(C+0.52)^-0.32 (10-shot) and the authors' note that the largest models start to fall behind the frontier.

rows.subject: ViT models
rows.operation_detail: Examined the ends of the compute-performance frontier.
rows.measure: Shape of error-rate versus compute curve
rows.value: The smallest models perform better than a power-law prediction at low compute; at high compute, the largest models do not approach zero error. The authors describe these as lower- and upper-end saturation.
rows.note: The authors describe an additive error constant and an x-axis shift as corresponding adjustments to the power-law form.
rows.check: Drop V7 (language-model fit-dependence). The saturation at both ends of compute is a qualification of the V5 power-law form in vision. The baseline is better stated as a pure power law E = aC^-b.

rows.subject: ViT Ti/16 and ViT L/16
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained; evaluated by few-shot transfer and fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of images seen needed to reach the same error rate.
rows.value: The Ti/16 model needs nearly 100 times more images than L/16 to match 10-shot representation quality; for fine-tuning, the factor is about 20.
rows.note: The paper reports the two evaluation settings separately in the text.
rows.check: Sample efficiency (images seen to reach equal error) is not the power-law form V5 names, and it does not concern language-model allocation (V3). Moved to fits_no_version.
